text.p: Australian Mark Phillippoussis, the man with the biggest serve in the game, upset 10th-seeded Andre Agassi of the U.S. 7-6 (7-5) 7-6 (7-5) in the first round of the Champions Cup on Tuesday.
There were two other men's upsets Tuesday, both in the second round. The top eight seeds received first-round byes.

The 49th-ranked Magnus Larsson of Sweden sent fifth-seeded Marcelo Rios of Chile packing 6-3 5-7 7-6 (7-2) in one match. Seventh-seeded Wayne Ferreira of South Africa was ousted 7-6 (7-5) 1-6 6-3 in the second round by 76th-ranked Gustavo Kuerten of Brazil.
Second seeded Thomas Muster of Austria and third-seeded and defending champion Michael Chang of the U.S. were more successful in second round matches Tuesday.
The second-ranked Muster easily defeated Adrian Voinea of Romania 6-2 6-4.
The third-ranked Chang posted a 6-4 6-3 second round victory over qualifier Sjeng Schalken of the Netherlands.

Chang led 4-1 in the first set, but let the 69th-ranked Schalken even the score to 4-4. Serving at 5-4, Chang won the first set on his second set point when a Schalken backhand half volley dropped into the net.
"I had a loose game there with a couple of double faults," Chang said of losing his serve in the seventh game. "It was not a good service game for me. He moves well for a big guy. He's talented."
In the second set, Chang faced two break points each on his serve in the third and fifth games, but escaped unscathed. He broke the Dutchman's serve in the second game.
The Agassi and Philippoussis battle was billed as a match between the the best server versus the best return of server.
Philippoussis, who won last week's Scottsdale event, served a record breaking 142 mph (228.5 kmh) ace at that Arizona based tournament.
"It's my biggest weapon, but I can hit winners with my forehand, backhand and come in and volley," Philippoussis said.
The Australian served 23 aces to Agassi's one in the match.
"It is a big serve," Agassi said. "I had my looks at break points. I certainly would be optimistic returning it again."
Agassi, a former No. 1 ranked player, who has a 5-8 won- loss record since playing the 1996 U.S. Open in September, has only competed in four tournaments this year.
"It is definitely about the intensity inside each point and the desire to want to win every point," Agassi said. "You know, I'm not just out there for the hell of it. My desire is definitely there."

The first set was an extremely tight competition in which neither player faced a break point on serve. Serving at 6-5 in the first set tiebreaker, Philippoussis won the set when Agassi dumped a forehand into the net.
In the second set, both players broke serve once as they headed for the face-off in the tiebreaker.
At 5-5 in the second set tiebreaker, Phillippoussis ended the match with two brilliant winners -- a 121 mph ace followed by a screeching forehand crosscourt passing shot.
"On the big points in the tiebreakers, I played well," Philippoussis said. "I went for some big winners."
